# The Kindness of Towers

## On lighthouses, strangers, and care that expects nothing back

There is a particular kind of building that exists entirely for people the builder will never meet. A house shelters its owners, a factory serves its shareholders, and a temple serves its congregation. A lighthouse serves whoever happens to be out there in the dark: the fisherman, the freighter captain, the frightened yachtsman who took a wrong turn at lunchtime. It does not know their names. It cannot see them. It cannot even be sure they exist on any given night. It simply stands on its rock and says, in the only language it has, *here, and not there.*

I have been thinking about lighthouses for a while, and I want to wander through them freely, because I think they hold an idea that is easy to miss, one about what it means to care for people at a distance and without reward.

### A tower on a sandbar

The oldest lighthouse everyone knows about is the one at Alexandria, the Pharos, built in the third century BC on a small island at the mouth of the harbor. The Egyptian coast there is a problem. It is low and flat, with almost nothing to steer by, and the approach is full of shoals. A sailor coming in from the Mediterranean could be a few miles from the greatest city in the world and not be able to see it. The Pharos was said to be well over a hundred meters tall, though the sources are inconsistent, and fire burned at its top with some arrangement of polished metal to throw the light farther. It stood for well over a thousand years, was shaken down piece by piece by earthquakes, and its last stones were eventually reused in a fortress built on the same spot.

The tower gave its name to the whole category. In French it is *phare*, in Italian *faro*, in Spanish *faro*, in Greek *fáros*. A whole family of languages decided that the word for "the thing that guides ships" should be the name of one particular tower. That is a kind of immortality. But I suspect the builders were thinking less about immortality than about grain ships. Alexandria was a commercial and political engine, and a lighthouse was infrastructure. Its generosity was real, but it was the generosity of an institution with reasons.

What interests me is that the reasons don't fully explain the structure. Once a light exists, it shines on everyone. You cannot build a beacon that guides only your own ships. The light falls on the rival's vessel and the enemy's vessel, and on the smuggler's, all equally. This is one of the strange properties of the lighthouse: it is a machine that can't discriminate. Economists have a dry term for such things, "non-excludable goods," and they have long used the lighthouse as a textbook example. There is a lively and slightly pedantic debate about whether lighthouses really were provided by the state or whether private parties collected fees at ports. Historians have pointed out, correctly, that in Britain a great many lights were built by private owners who were licensed to charge passing ships. Fine. But even the fee collectors were charging for something that they could not, in the moment, withhold.

### The man who died in his own tower

Building a lighthouse on a rock in the open sea is one of the most difficult things human beings have tried to do with stone, and the history of it is largely a history of stubbornness.

Consider the Eddystone Rocks, a reef off the coast of Cornwall that has been wrecking ships since there were ships to wreck. In the late 1690s a man named Henry Winstanley, an eccentric with a taste for mechanical marvels, decided to build a light on it. His tower was a fanciful, ornate, half-timbered thing, more like a pavilion than a fortification, and against expectation it survived several winters. Winstanley was proud enough of it that he said he wished to be inside it during "the greatest storm there ever was in England," so that he could see what it could endure.

In November 1703, he got his wish. The Great Storm, which really was among the worst in English history, flattened the tower. Winstanley was inside. Nothing was left the next morning except a few twisted iron bars.

I find this story both awful and instructive, because what happened next is the more remarkable part. Other people built another one. And when that one burned down, as a wooden one eventually did, a man named John Smeaton, an engineer who wasn't even very interested in lighthouses beforehand, studied the problem and concluded that the tower should be shaped like an oak tree: wide at the base, curving inward as it rose, so that it would resist the sea the way a trunk resists wind. He cut the granite blocks so that they interlocked with dovetail joints, and he experimented until he found a form of lime that would set underwater. His tower, finished in 1759, stood for more than a century. When the rock beneath it began to erode, the upper part was carefully dismantled and re-erected on land at Plymouth, where it still stands as a monument. The stump of it remains out on the rock.

That is a kind of relay. Winstanley's death did not stop the project. Each failure was studied by the next person, who had never met the previous one and would never meet the next. The tower was as much an accumulation of knowledge across time as it was a structure in space.

### The Stevensons and the inheritance of duty

Nowhere is that clearer than in the Stevenson family of Scotland. Robert Stevenson built the Bell Rock light, out in the North Sea off Angus, finished in 1810, on a reef that was submerged at high tide, so that work could occur only during a few hours of low water each day, and the workmen had to be ferried in and out through the swell. His son, and then his grandsons, went on to design dozens of lighthouses around Scotland. It was a dynasty of engineers whose work consisted of standing in the worst weather Britain has to offer and asking what shape a tower should be.

The most famous member of the family, of course, never did the work. Robert Louis Stevenson was expected to become a lighthouse engineer too, and instead became a writer, because he was sickly and restless and wanted to tell stories. His father was disappointed. But Stevenson wrote later, with what reads to me as real tenderness, about the family trade. He said he was proud of belonging to a line of men who had made "the great lights" that saved lives. He understood, I think, that what his ancestors had done was a form of literature: a sentence written in stone and glass whose meaning was *be careful, someone has thought of you.*

### The lens

The technology of the light itself went through its own quiet revolution. For centuries, lights had been open fires, then candles and oil lamps set in front of reflectors, wasteful and weak. In 1822 a French physicist named Augustin-Jean Fresnel, who was more interested in the nature of light than in shipping, built a new kind of lens. Instead of a single thick slab of glass, which would have been absurdly heavy at the size required, he used concentric rings of prisms, each ring angled so that it bent the light into a parallel beam. Nearly all of the lamp's output was gathered and thrown out toward the horizon.

If you have never stood next to a large Fresnel lens, it is hard to convey what it looks like. It is a beehive of glass, taller than a person, cut into ridges and facets, each catching the daylight and scattering it in tiny rainbows. It looks less like an instrument than like jewelry made for a giant. It was, however, a completely practical object, designed by mathematics and ground by hand, and it multiplied the reach of a flame by an order of magnitude. Some of these lenses floated on a bath of mercury so that a modest clockwork mechanism could rotate them with almost no friction. The keepers wound the clockwork by hand, like a grandfather clock, every few hours through the night.

The pulses of light that result, the flash pattern, are what turn a lighthouse from a mere lamp into a word. Every light has its own "character": two flashes every ten seconds, one long flash every six, and so on, recorded in books that every navigator carries. A sailor who sees a light does not merely see a light. He counts, checks the chart, and learns exactly which tower he is looking at, and therefore exactly where he is. Each lighthouse is a sentence with a single message: *I am here. I am this one. You are near me.*

### The keepers

And then there were the people who lived in them.

The keeper's life was a peculiar mixture of boredom and vigilance. Journals survive from many stations, and they are astonishingly repetitive: *Wind NW, fresh. Trimmed the lamp. Painted the gallery rail. Fog signal ran seven hours.* Then, once in a great while, something like: *Vessel ashore on the south ledge. Rowed out with assistant. Took off eleven men.* The mundane entries and the heroic ones sit side by side in the same handwriting, with the same flat tone, as if rescuing eleven men were one more chore in the day's list.

There is a lot of romance about keepers, and some of it is deserved, but I'm also drawn to the unromantic part. The keeper had to keep the light burning *every night*, regardless of mood, illness, loneliness, or the fact that no ship might pass. A light that goes out for one night in a hundred is worse than no light, because sailors will have learned to trust it. The whole value of the thing lies in its reliability. This is a moral situation of an unusual kind: a duty owed to no one in particular, enforced by no one who is watching, and whose failure would only ever be discovered after a disaster.

The legend of the Flannan Isles is the dark mirror of this. In December 1900, the relief boat arrived at a lighthouse on a remote Scottish island group and found all three keepers gone. The clock had stopped, a meal was apparently half-eaten, and one set of oilskins was missing. The likeliest explanation is mundane and terrible: a freak wave swept them from a landing platform. But the story has been embroidered into ghost lore, songs, and poems, because the image is so haunting: a lamp, a table, a light that had been faithfully burning for someone else, and nobody home.

### Automation, and what it costs

Today, almost all lighthouses are automated. The Fresnel lenses have mostly been replaced with LED beacons, or with small, efficient optics that need almost no supervision, and the ships that pass carry GPS and radar and electronic charts. The last keeper left the Scottish lights in the late 1990s. A few stations elsewhere, in Canada for instance, still have staff on some remote rocks, partly for safety and partly because human eyes are useful in bad weather.

It would be easy to be sentimental about this, and I want to resist being *only* sentimental. Automation is, in a real sense, a triumph. A keeper's life was dangerous and isolating, and the families who lived at those stations sometimes paid for the job with their sanity. If a sensor can do the work, then good.

But something is lost that is hard to name. The manned lighthouse was a place where care was embodied. When a ship saw the light, there was, in principle, a person behind it. Someone had climbed the stairs, someone was awake. The light was a sign of attention, and the attention was human. An automated beacon has no such backing. It may be even more reliable, but it does not *mean* the same thing. It is a signal without a signaler.

I don't say this to argue that we should bring the keepers back. I say it because it points to a general pattern in modern life: the more efficiently we automate our care for strangers, the more invisible that care becomes, and the easier it is to forget that anyone ever chose to provide it.

### The ethics of the unreturned favor

Here is what I think the lighthouse teaches, and it is not really about the sea.

Most of our moral thinking is organized around reciprocity: I help you, you help me, and we keep a rough ledger. This is not a bad system. It is how trust gets built, and it's the basis of nearly all commerce and friendship. But there is a second kind of moral act that does not fit the ledger at all, which is the act of doing something useful for people who cannot repay you, who may never know you did it, and whom you will never meet.

You can see the shape of this everywhere once you start looking. Someone plants a tree they will never sit under. Someone maintains a trail, clearing fallen branches so that a hiker two months from now doesn't trip. Someone writes a careful answer to a stranger's question on a public forum, at midnight, for no reason except that the answer is right and the question was sincere. Someone leaves a cairn at a fork in the path. Someone puts a bench at the top of a hill, with a small plaque, in memory of a person who liked the view. These are all lighthouses. They are small structures of attention, built for the benefit of an anonymous future.

What makes them remarkable is that they are *legible* only to those who need them. A lighthouse is invisible to the person asleep in a warm bed inland. It becomes the most important object in the world for the person who is lost. Its value is unevenly distributed in exactly the way that need is, concentrated at the moment of danger and absent otherwise. This is why so much of the best public good is under-appreciated. The people it helps most are, by definition, the people who were in trouble, and people in trouble are not usually in a position to write thank-you letters. Often they never even realize what saved them. The ship simply turns at the right moment, and the sailor thinks only, *there's the light, I'm fine.*

### The light says only one thing

There is one more thing I love about lighthouses, and it is their restraint. A lighthouse doesn't tell you where to go. It doesn't say "turn left" or "the harbor is that way, please follow me." It says only where the danger is, or where you are, and leaves the rest to you. It respects the sailor's competence. The information it gives is minimal, honest, and true, and then it falls silent and lets the person steer.

That, to me, is a good model for helping anyone. The best help does not take over. It offers a fixed point, a reliable fact, a place to stand while the other person works out their own course. It makes no demands and creates no dependency. It just holds still, and burns, and lets the traveler use it as they see fit. A good teacher does this, and so does a good friend, and so does a good map. So, when it works, does a good answer to a hard question.

### Coda: a thought experiment

Imagine you are on a small boat at night. The sea is a dark, heaving nothing. The sky has clouded over. You have been sailing for hours and you are tired in the way that makes small errors feel enormous. Then, far off on the horizon, a point of light appears, then vanishes, then appears again. You count: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight — flash. You look it up. It is what you hoped it was.

In that moment, you are not thinking about the engineer who designed the tower, or the mason who cut the stones, or the family that spent three generations perfecting the shape, or the glassmaker who ground the prisms, or the keeper who trimmed the wick on a night like this one a hundred and fifty years ago. But all of them are in that flash. It is the visible tip of an enormous, invisible cooperation, a long chain of people who decided, without ever meeting you, that you should get home.

That is the kindness of towers. It is a kindness that scales across centuries and requires no gratitude. And it seems to me that most of what is best in any civilization has that same shape: something built patiently by people who will never see the ones it saves, and left burning, quietly, at the edge of the dark.

If I could ask one thing of the world, it might be that we build more of them. Not necessarily of stone. But of whatever material our own particular coast requires: some steady, honest signal, placed where it will do the most good, maintained through bad weather, and offered to any stranger who happens to need it.
